cells.tense: You are raising the frame while the thing inside it is still growing.
cells.act: wait until you know which part matters, then begin with that part
cells.ask: Before one caring task this week, hold off until the part that matters most becomes clear, then start with that one. Let the rest wait its turn.
cells.core:
You're raising the frame while the thing inside it is still growing. What you tend takes shape from you — a form to hold the worry, the meetings, the days. Things make sense in your presence, and that isn't the point of it; it's the byproduct.

What's working is the patience, and the asking is to keep feeding it. The part you feel sure of is rarely the part that matters most, and a direct knowing can be trusted before it can be defended. Wait until the important part shows itself, then pick it up. The waiting isn't idling — it's the crafting, and it lets the rest stay unmanaged without anything being lost.

cells.tense: You are planning the shape of something whose size you cannot yet know.
cells.act: step back far enough to see the whole arrangement
cells.ask: Once this week, step back from something you're shaping until you can see its whole arrangement, and name what holds it up without adding anything.
cells.core:
You're planning the shape of something before its size is known. The structures you keep making are tight and real, but the frame has begun standing where the living thing goes, and whatever grows inside has to fit itself to the walls.

What's working is the eye for pattern; the ask is to step back from one arrangement and take in the whole shape of it, without adding anything. No restructuring, no fixes. Just look at what's there, including the part that hasn't grown into its slot yet. The distance lets you catch problems early, and your structures can serve what they hold again instead of explaining it away.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door you already walked through, waiting for the pieces to be handed over.
cells.act: let one structure collapse that could not hold
cells.ask: Pick one setup that only stands because you're propping it — one you know rests on a premise that isn't true — and stop holding it. Watch what comes down, and leave the ground bare.
cells.core:
You're standing at a door you already walked through, waiting for the pieces to be handed over. What you care about is real and scattered; the ordering doesn't happen, and nothing gets carried forward. It isn't a matter of caring more — the shape hasn't been made.

What isn't yours to fix is the organizing that didn't come. Pick one structure that only holds because you're propping it, and stop holding it. Watch it come down. What falls was false anyway; what's left is the actual ground, and you'll see what matters from there. Don't rebuild in the gap yet — leave things unfilled, and there's no hurry.

cells.tense: You are setting the table each day without noticing your hand is the one arranging it.
cells.act: let the thing end that is already over
cells.ask: When something you're tending has already stopped — a practice, a routine, a way you meet someone — stop giving it a slot. Let it be finished.
cells.core:
You're setting the table each day without noticing your hand is the one arranging it. Others lean on the shape you make — the routines, the order, the way a week is set up — and to you it looks like nothing in particular. You feel formless while the form is coming from you.

The honest act is to let one thing end that has already ended. There's often a practice or habit kept going out of a sense of care, and its time is done. Name it, and stop it. What ends stays honoured; what's inside the structure you built gets room to grow. The ending is yours, done quietly, with no announcement, and it's the clearest proof that the arranging was your work.
